title: International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg: Judgment of 30 September and 1 October 1946 on the plunder of public and private property and works of art in occupied territories
body: International Military Tribunal (Nuremberg), established by the London Agreement of 8 August 1945
summary: The International Military Tribunal sat at Nuremberg to try the major German war criminals. Article 6(b) of its Charter listed "plunder of public or private property" among war crimes, and Count Three of the Indictment (lodged 18 October 1945) charged the defendants with war crimes including a section titled "Plunder of Public and Private Property". In its Judgment of 30 September and 1 October 1946 the Tribunal stated that "a wholesale seizure was made of art treasures, furniture, textiles and similar articles in all the invaded countries" and described the work of the Einsatzstab Rosenberg in seizing cultural treasures. Of Rosenberg it found that he "is responsible for a system of organised plunder of both public and private property throughout the invaded countries of Europe" and that he "is guilty on all four counts". The Judgment also made findings on plunder or pillage in respect of Goering and Seyss-Inquart. This entry covers only the plunder findings; the Judgment's wider findings on the defendants are not summarised.
legal_basis: The Charter (annexed to the London Agreement of 8 August 1945) gave the Tribunal power to try persons for, among other things, war crimes. Article 6(b) defines war crimes as "violations of the laws or customs of war" and says such violations "shall include, but not be limited to" a list that includes "plunder of public or private property, wanton destruction of cities, towns or villages, or devastation not justified by military necessity". In the section of the Judgment on the law relating to war crimes, the Tribunal cited Articles 46, 50, 52 and 56 of the Hague Convention of 1907 (the page read does not cite Article 47), stated that the crimes defined by Article 6(b) were already recognised as war crimes under international law, and stated that by 1939 the Convention's rules were recognised by all civilised nations as "declaratory of the laws and customs of war"; it also said that individual liability for such violations was "too well settled to admit of argument". The Indictment's Count Three, section on plunder, cited "particularly Articles 46 to 56 inclusive of the Hague Regulations, 1907". The text of the Hague Regulations themselves was not read for this entry.
outcome: In the Judgment of 30 September and 1 October 1946: (1) The Tribunal stated that "a wholesale seizure was made of art treasures, furniture, textiles and similar articles in all the invaded countries", that the Einsatzstab Rosenberg's work developed into "a project for the seizure of cultural treasures", and that "In many of the occupied countries private collections were robbed, libraries were plundered, and private houses were pillaged." (2) Rosenberg: the Tribunal stated he "is responsible for a system of organised plunder of both public and private property throughout the invaded countries of Europe", that as of 14 July 1944 more than 21,903 art objects had been seized by the Einsatzstab in the West, and that he is "guilty on all four counts". (3) Goering: the Tribunal found him guilty on all four counts; the Judgment states that he "was the active authority in the spoliation" of conquered territory. The Goering section as read does not mention works of art or the Einsatzstab. (4) Seyss-Inquart: the Tribunal stated that in the Netherlands "there was widespread pillage of public and private property", given "colour of legality" by his regulations, and found him guilty under Counts Two, Three and Four (not guilty on Count One). (5) Frank: the proceedings record a finding of not guilty on Count One and guilty on Counts Three and Four; the Frank section of the Judgment was not read for plunder findings. (6) Sentences: a mirror of the official proceedings volume records death by hanging for Goering, Rosenberg, Frank and Seyss-Inquart. The Judgment does not, in the sections read, attribute any single conviction to the plunder of cultural property alone.

timeline.title: Rosenberg designated by Hitler
timeline.description: The Judgment states that "The defendant Rosenberg was designated by Hitler on the 29th January 1940" as head of a Centre for National Socialist Ideological and Educational Research, and that thereafter the organisation known as the "Einsatzstab Rosenberg" conducted its operations on a very great scale. The Judgment says it was originally designed for a research library and "developed into a project for the seizure of cultural treasures."

timeline.title: Further decree on searching cultural establishments
timeline.description: The Judgment states that on 1 March 1942 Hitler issued a further decree authorising Rosenberg to search libraries, lodges and cultural establishments, and that Rosenberg's activities were thereafter extended to the occupied countries.

timeline.title: Einsatzstab seizure figure cited in the Judgment
timeline.description: In the section on Rosenberg the Judgment states that as of 14 July 1944 "more than 21,903 art objects, including famous paintings and museum pieces," had been seized by the Einsatzstab in the West.

timeline.title: London Agreement and Charter
timeline.description: The Judgment begins its account with the Agreement of 8 August 1945 establishing the Tribunal, to which the Charter is annexed. Article 6(b) of the Charter lists "plunder of public or private property" among the violations of the laws or customs of war.

timeline.title: Indictment lodged
timeline.description: The Judgment states the Indictment was lodged against the defendants in Berlin on 18 October 1945; the trial record of the first day gives the same date. Count Three of the Indictment charged war crimes, including a section headed "Plunder of Public and Private Property" that cites Articles 46 to 56 of the Hague Regulations (1907).

timeline.title: Trial begins
timeline.description: The Judgment states the trial began on 20 November 1945; the proceedings volume records the first day as Tuesday, 20 November 1945.

timeline.title: Reading of the Judgment begins
timeline.description: On the 217th day of the trial the President announced that the Judgment would be read. The Judgment is dated 30 September and 1 October 1946.

timeline.title: Verdicts and sentences
timeline.description: The proceedings record guilty verdicts on all four counts for Goering and Rosenberg, and for Frank on Counts Three and Four; the Seyss-Inquart section of the Judgment finds him guilty under Counts Two, Three and Four. A mirror of the official volume gives the sentence for Goering, Rosenberg, Frank and Seyss-Inquart as death by hanging.

changelog.change: Initial draft. case_type TRIBUNAL chosen (an ad hoc international military tribunal created by treaty), consistent with the approved Strugar entry; INTERNATIONAL_CRIMINAL would also be defensible. Dates: Indictment lodged 18 Oct 1945 and trial opened 20 Nov 1945 (Judgment title page and trial record); Judgment dated 30 Sept and 1 Oct 1946. Known gaps: (1) direct curl to avalon.law.yale.edu was refused by the proxy and several Avalon URLs (count3.asp, judfrank.asp, judcont.asp) were not opened; all pages were read through a summarising fetch tool, so quotations must be re-verified verbatim against the pages. (2) Article 6 of the Charter was read only in fragments (the 6(b) lead-in and the plunder clause); the full article text was not reproduced and the Charter's own page does not carry a date. (3) Indictment Count Three was read on a Britannica-hosted mirror of the Avalon text (tier 2). (4) Sentences come from a Mazal Library mirror of Blue Series vol. 1 p. 366 (tier 2); the Avalon 1 October page read did not reach the sentences or the Seyss-Inquart verdict. (5) The Frank section of the Judgment was not opened for plunder findings; Frank appears only through the verdict record. (6) The Goering section as read mentions neither works of art nor the Einsatzstab; the Goering/art link frequently asserted elsewhere is therefore NOT claimed. (7) Hague Convention (1907) and Regulations texts were not read; the Judgment cites Articles 46, 50, 52 and 56 (not 47), the Indictment 46 to 56. (8) The Scholz-report figures and the Posse report passage in the Judgment were seen only as fragments and are not used. (9) The Judgment's separate findings on Counts One, Two and Four are not covered. Interpretation left null: no attributable analysis was opened.

Independent verification against Avalon pages (Charter, Judgment title page, law section, war-crimes section, Rosenberg, Goering, Seyss-Inquart, 20 Nov 1945 and 1 Oct 1946 proceedings, Count Three mirror, Mazal mirror). Confirmed: Art. 6(b) wording; Agreement date 8 Aug 1945; Indictment lodged in Berlin 18 Oct 1945; trial began 20 Nov 1945; Judgment dated 30 Sept and 1 Oct 1946; Hague Convention Arts. 46, 50, 52, 56 cited (not 47); Indictment cites Arts. 46 to 56; Rosenberg and Goering guilty on all four counts; Frank not guilty Count One, guilty Counts Three and Four; Seyss-Inquart guilty Counts Two, Three, Four, not guilty Count One; Goering section has no art/Einsatzstab mention; death-by-hanging sentences per Mazal mirror. Fix (2 edits): the 21,903 art objects figure is stated in the Judgment as seized 'by the Einsatzstab in the West'; added 'in the West' in outcome and timeline. Not verified: Seyss-Inquart verdict/sentence on the Avalon 1 Oct page (truncated or not reached); Hague texts; Frank Judgment section. No evaluative wording found.
